INTEREST OF THE AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae America’s Future, founded in 1946,
is one of America’s oldest policy-oriented nonprofit
organizations.  It is exempt from federal income tax
under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code.
This amicus participates in the public policy process,
including conducting research, and informing and
educating the public on the proper construction of state
and federal constitutions, as well as statutes related to
the rights of citizens, and questions related to human
and civil rights secured by law.   This amicus has filed
many amicus briefs in immigration-related cases.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
 Petitioners in this case are two aliens who have
been present in the United States for decades.  Tamer
Wassily, an Egyptian, entered in 1993 on a tourist
visa, which he overstayed, while Byron Velasquez
Arreaga, a Guatemalan, entered in 1995. Both were
illegally present in the United States when they were
granted asylum by immigration judges in 2000 and
1996, respectively.
After an alien has been granted asylum, he may be
eligible for adjustment of status.  Under 8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b), the Secretary of Homeland Security or the
1  It is hereby certified that no counsel for a party authored this
brief in whole or in part; and that no person other than this
amicus curiae, its members, or its counsel made a monetary
contribution to its preparation or submission.

2
Attorney General,2 in his discretion and subject to
additional regulations, “may adjust to the status of an
alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the
status of any alien granted asylum.”
Both Petitioners, while in the United States under
asylee status, were subsequently convicted of serious
crimes:  Wassily in 2004 of stalking in the third degree
and child endangerment, and Velasquez Arreaga in
2015 of driving while intoxicated and in 2018 of
aggravated driving while intoxicated.
Subsequently, for each Petitioner, an Immigration
Judge (“IJ”) found those convictions to meet the
threshold of “particularly serious crime” in 8 U.S.C.
§ 1158(b)(2)(A)(ii) and terminated Wassily and
Velasquez Arreaga’s asylee status on September 3,
2008 and July 1, 2019, respectively.  Wassily also
received a second look from an IJ, who again
determined that his crime met the “particularly
serious” threshold, but nonetheless granted a waiver of
inadmissibility and adjustment of status.  See In re
Wassily, No. A026-102-429 (U.S. Immgr. Ct. Oct. 21,
2019).
Both Petitioners filed appeals leading to multiple
decisions by the Board of Immigration Appeals.  In the
case of Wassily:  on June 14, 2010, dismissing
2  Prior to enactment of the “Emergency Supplemental
Appropriations Act for Defense, the Global War on Terror, and
Tsunami Relief, 2005,” 119 Stat. 231 (May 11, 2005), the power to
designate a person as a refugee was vested exclusively in the

3
administrative appeal;  on June 4, 2014, remanding to
the IJ for further proceedings; and on April 27, 2022,
vacating the second IJ decision.  In the case of
Velasquez Arreaga, on December 11, 2020, the Board
of Immigration Appeals  affirmed the IJ’s denial of
adjustment of status, and on March 23, 2023, the
Board dismissed Velasquez Arreaga’s appeal.
In the decision now under review, the Second
Circuit explained its interpretation of the key statute,
as follows:
Velasquez Arreaga, Wassily, and the dissent
all advance an interpretation of 8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b) that makes little sense:  A noncitizen
convicted of a particularly serious crime,
and whose asylum status was terminated
as a result, would categorically be treated the
same as a noncitizen with current asylum
status when applying to adjust to lawful
permanent resident status.  The termination of
the noncitizen’s asylum status would simply be
irrelevant. It would be one thing if this
peculiar result were required by the statute.
U n su r p r i s i n g l y ,  th o u g h ,  such  a
counterintuitive interpretation of the statutory
scheme can be reached only by disregarding
the clear meaning of the statutory text.
[Wassily v. Bondi, 150 F.4th 100, 109 (2d Cir.
2025) (“Wassily”) (emphasis added).]
The circuit court then ruled that because “Wassily’s
and Velasquez Arreaga’s asylum status was
terminated, they were not eligible to adjust to lawful

4
permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b),”
and thus denied the petitions for review.  Wassily at
109.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Petitioners have not made their case, using either
text, context, or purpose, that 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b)
should be interpreted to make the termination of an
asylee’s status irrelevant to whether they may
continue on a path to lawful permanent resident status
and possibly citizenship.  Here, termination resulted
from Petitioners’ commission of “particularly serious
crimes.”  Another reason for which asylee status can be
terminated is that the asylee status was obtained by
fraud.
The reading of the statute advanced by the
Government is fully consistent with the purpose of the
statute — that there should be a special asylee
pathway to lawful permanent residence — but that
pathway should only apply to persons who have not
been stripped of the status which qualifies them to be
on that pathway.  It is and should be irrelevant that an
alien once had asylee status, as only current asylee
status is relevant.  Additionally, there is no policy
justification to read § 1159(b) as granting rights to
persons who are no longer asylees, as they are no
longer protected refugees under the terms of the 1951
Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees on
which the Refugee Act of 1980 was based.
Lawful permanent resident status is a way station
on the path to citizenship, and there is no reason to

5
believe that it should be granted to persons not
currently viewed as asylees.  Such matters should not
be left to the discretion of some Attorney General who
may grant that status liberally, based on a belief in
open borders.  Neither lawful permanent resident
status nor citizenship should be given away so cheaply.
Additionally, the sad truth is that thousands of
aliens have gamed the system, with the help of many
immigration lawyers and NGO’s, to obtain asylee
status through fraud.  Therefore, this Court cannot
assume that all those once given asylee status
originally met the statutory qualification for refugee
status.  The termination of asylee status is significant,
and that person, by law, no longer can be treated as
being on the pathway to lawful permanent resident
status and possibly citizenship.
ARGUMENT
I. THE INTERPRETATION ADVANCED BY
PETITIONERS IS INCONSISTENT WITH
BOTH THE TEXT AND THE PURPOSE OF
THE STATUTE.
The question presented is whether noncitizens who
were granted asylum, which was then terminated, are
still eligible for adjustment to “lawful permanent
residence” under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b). That statute
provides in its most relevant part:
The Secretary of Homeland Security or the
Attorney General, in the Secretary’s or the
Attorney General’s discretion ... may adjust to

6
the status of an alien lawfully admitted for
permanent residence the status of any alien
granted asylum who [meets five further
requirements3].
The Government takes the position that the phrase
“any alien granted asylum” includes only those aliens
who currently have asylee status.  Wassily takes the
position that  “any alien granted asylum” includes any
alien who at anytime in the past was granted asylum,
even after that status has been terminated, and even
if that termination was for committing a “particularly
serious crime.”  This amicus believes that the only
reasonable reading of this text is that to qualify for an
additional benefit of being granted lawful permanent
residence (“LPR”), the alien must currently have asylee
status.  Those who lost that status are no longer in the
category of persons that Congress wanted to assist.
The Government has presented a compelling
argument based on  the text and context of the law,
applying relevant canons of construction, which this
amicus believes demonstrates the correctness of its
position, and does not seek to add to those arguments.
3 These five requirements are:
“(1) applies for such adjustment,
(2) has been physically present in the United States for at least
one year after being granted asylum,
(3) continues to be a refugee within the meaning of section
1101(a)(42)(A) of this title or a spouse or child of such a refugee,
(4) is not firmly resettled in any foreign country, and
(5) is admissible (except as otherwise provided under subsection
(c)) as an immigrant under this chapter at the time of
examination for adjustment of such alien.”

7
Rather this brief addresses the purpose and history of
the statute in question.
The purpose of the statute was raised by
Petitioners, seeking to show that their interpretation
of § 1159(b) furthers the  congressional desire to
increase the discretion of the Attorney General.  Brief
for Petitioners (“Pet. Br.”) at 35.  The Government
disputes this argument, explaining that Petitioners’
argument “suggest[s] barriers to the statute’s
operation that do not exist.”  Brief for the Respondent
(“Resp. Br.”) at 34.  Petitioners’ suggestion of a
congressional purpose misses the mark, as it ignores
the rather obvious reason as to why Congress would
want only those with current asylum status to be
benefitted by being able to convert to lawful
permanent resident status.
It appears clear that Congress wanted to keep the
special asylee pathway to lawful permanent residence
open, not for all facing persecution, but only for those
who were entitled to protection from persecution.
8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) was added by the Refugee Act of
1980, 94 Stat. 102 (Mar. 17, 1980).  That statutory
provision was based on the 1951 Convention Relating
to the Status of Refugees (April 22, 1954) and its 1967
Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees.4  Although
the United States did not ratify the 1951 Convention,
many of its provisions were incorporated into law in
the Refugee Act of 1980.
4  American Immigration Council, “An Overview of U.S. Refugee
Law and Policy” (April 2025).

8
The Convention’s Article 33, entitled
“PROHIBITION OF EXPULSION OR RETURN
(‘REFOULEMENT’)” states:
1. No Contracting State shall expel or
return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner
whatsoever to the frontiers of territories
where his life or freedom would be
threatened on account of his race, religion,
nationality, membership of a particular social
group or political opinion.  [Emphasis added.]
The obvious implication is that once the refugee’s life
or freedom is no longer threatened, he may have his
refugee status terminated and be returned.  In that
case, he no longer needs either asylee status or “lawful
permanent residence.”  The next provision of the
Convention shows that more is required of a refugee
than just facing a credible threat of persecution.
2. The benefit of the present provision may
not, however, be claimed by a refugee whom
there are reasonable grounds for regarding as
a danger to the security of the country in
which he is, or who, having been convicted by
a final judgment of a particularly serious
crime, constitutes a danger to the community
of that country.
This latter provision is identical to the statutory
provision barring those who committed a  “particularly
serious crime” from refugee status.  Both of these
provisions of the Convention indicate that refugee
status is neither permanent, nor a vested right to

9
remain in the host country.  Neither should judges
artificially create a vested right to remain here under
lawful permanent resident status regardless of
behavior, as Petitioners argue.
Protection of refugees was to be temporary,
triggered by the existence of the risks of serious
persecution, and normally refugee status would end
when the risk ended.  It was designed to assist persons
who continue to be refugees, not just that they at some
time in the past they had refugee status.  If
circumstances resolved in the individual’s home
country, the refugee status would no longer be needed,
and therefore, could return the their home country.
Certainly, there would be no need for the person to be
given lawful permanent resident status in the United
States.  Additionally, if an individual had refugee
status in the past, but lost it due to fraud or
commission of a “particularly serious crime,” then they
would not be eligible for the favorable treatment that
Congress provided for those with valid continuing
refugee status.
In either event, there is no indication that if an
individual had once in the past had refugee status, but
no longer does, whether due to the fact persecution is
not continuing, or to the discovery he obtained that
status by fraud, or due to commission of a particularly
serious crime, he has a lifetime pass to apply for lawful
permanent resident status.  Section 1159(b) did not
create a new immigration program, but addressed a
problem that was specific to refugees, so long as they
were actually refugees, and had not lost that status.
There is no basis to view a past asylum grant as

10
creating a vested, lifetime right, allowing that person
to remain on a permanent basis.
II. LAWFUL PERMANENT RESIDENT STATUS
IS A STEP TOWARD CITIZENSHIP THAT IS
NOT AVAILABLE TO THOSE WHOSE
BEHAVIOR CAUSED A REVOCATION OF
THEIR ASYLEE STATUS.
Both the Second Circuit and the Respondent’s brief
explain how, in the statutory scheme, § 1159(b) can
lead to lawful permanent residence, which can lead to
citizenship.  The Second Circuit states “a grant of
asylum also opens a path to citizenship” as follows.
Under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b), a noncitizen who
“has been physically present in the United
States for at least one year after being granted
asylum....”  Once granted lawful permanent
resident status....  Assuming other conditions
are met, 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b) provides that the
Secretary of Homeland Security or the
Attorney General “may adjust to the status of
an alien lawfully admitted for permanent
residence the status of any alien granted
asylum.”  Once granted lawful permanent
resident status, a noncitizen may ultimately
apply for citizenship through naturalization.
[Wassily at 101-02.]
Respondent’s brief correctly describes lawful
permanent resident status as “a discretionary
immigration benefit that is a step along the path to
citizenship.”  Resp. Br. at 38.    Under 8 U.S.C.

11
§ 1427(a), naturalization is conditioned in part on an
alien residing continuously in the United States for at
least five years after “‘being lawfully admitted for
permanent residence.’”  Id.  “U.S. citizenship is the
ultimate protection against removal, and aliens with
lawful-permanent-resident status may attempt to
naturalize to avoid removal proceedings, just as
petitioners here sought to adjust their status.”  Id. at
39.
To many foreigners, U.S. citizenship is not just
“the ultimate protection against removal,” but the
“ultimate goal” for their lives.  Many aliens will do all
they can, often counseled by “public interest” lawyers
seeking to open the borders of our nation to all comers,
to say all the right things to get asylee status to get on
a pathway to citizenship.  Many fabricate claims of
persecution in their home country, having no
compunction against committing fraud on our system,
if they want citizenship for them and their family
badly enough. Our system should be based on the
understanding that many aliens will do whatever is
required to get on and stay on that path to citizenship.
If a person is caught committing fraud, and then
has asylee status terminated, that person should be
taken off the path to citizenship, as the Government
contends, not allowed to continue on that path as
Petitioners demand.  If a person commits a
particularly serious crime, he has not just forfeited his
place on that pathway to citizenship, but he has also
forfeited refugee status, fully consistent with the 1951
Convention.  There is no permanent benefit to be
gained from once having been determined to be a

12
refugee.  Once a person no longer qualifies for that
status, he should be removed from the path to lawful
permanent residence, and to citizenship.
III.PETITIONERS SEEK TO HAVE THE COURTS
RE-INTERPRET A FEDERAL LAW TO
BENEFIT MANY WHO HAVE COMMITTED
FRAUD OR PARTICULARLY SERIOUS
CRIMES.
Petitioners advance a curious statutory
interpretation that the Government’s termination of
their asylee status, for good and valid reasons, should
have no relevance to their eligibility for “lawful
permanent residence,” and from there a path to
“citizenship.”  With that difficult interpretive hill to
climb, it is no surprise that Petitioners have appealed
to sympathy.  However, Petitioners’ emotional
argument is no better than their statutory construction
argument.   Petitioners argument reads like a plea
before sentencing for a crime:
Under the government’s [reading of 8 U.S.C.
§ 1159(b)] noncitizens who have lived in the
United States for decades — who have built
careers, raised families, paid taxes, and
contributed to their communities — face
removal to countries where they still fear
persecution or where they have no ties. That
includes innocent refugees and spouses and
children of refugees whose asylum is
terminated through no fault of their own.
[Pet. Br. at 4 (emphasis added).]

13
The argument that these Petitioners are just
“innocent refugees” who are being punished “through
no fault of their own” certainly has no relevance here,
where these particular Petitioners have been convicted
of committing “particularly serious crimes.”  As
discussed in section II, supra, under the 1951
Convention which the Refugee Act was tracking, there
were two express limitations to refugee status:  where
there were “reasonable grounds” to view the person as
“a danger to the security of the [host] country” or
conviction of “a particularly serious crime.”  Such
persons are not entitled to sympathy, as under the
Convention, refugee status “may not ... be claimed” by
such a person.  Petitioners now wish to avoid those
limitations on the benefits of refugee status by
invoking the interests of family members, but the
consequences of a person’s actions always spill over to
family members.  Our system of justice does not allow
a criminal to evade responsibility for his actions
because he has a family, or because he claims to have
been a good citizen who paid his taxes.
However, there is another reality of the refugee
system as it has operated in recent years which this
Court should not ignore.  The rules, including the
statute in question here, were written in the belief that
persons would not obtain refugee status to begin with
without being fully entitled to that status.  The reality
is quite different.  An unknown, but substantial,
number of asylum applicants have been given that
status without meeting the high statutory standards
by gaming the system, facilitated by prior
Administrations which did not believe that borders
should be kept secure.  Were the over 170,000 persons

14
who made their way to the United States and who
were given refugee status during a recent four year
period (discussed infra), all really refugees under the
law?  There is good reason to believe that many were
not.
A report  published by the Center for Immigration
Studies, “Fraud in the ‘Credible Fear’ Process,” noted:
[b]ecause of ... the difficulty that U.S.
Citizenship and Immigration Services
(USCIS), U.S. Immigration and Customs
Enforcement (ICE) attorneys, and immigration
judges face in effectively identifying fraud in
the asylum application process, asylum
can be readily abused by aliens who are
not legally eligible for that benefit.”5
The report notes that “[a]liens with ties to terrorist
organizations have attempted to enter illegally and
claim asylum fraudulently.  Hundreds of aliens to
whom the terrorist bar to asylum may apply have been
found to have a credible fear.”  Id.
The attention of the media in recent months has
been directed to well-documented massive fraud by
Somali immigrants in Minnesota.  One of those
involved is Omar Jamal, who, as it turns out, had filed
a fraudulent asylum application that gained him
permanent presence in the United States.
5 Andrew Arthur, “Fraud in the ‘Credible Fear’ Process,” Center
for Immigration Studies (Apr. 2017).

15
Born in Somalia’s capital city of Mogadishu,
Jamal secured asylum status in the U.S. in
1998 under false pretenses by denying that he
ever was granted permanent residency or
asylum in any other country.  Jamal gained
refugee and permanent resident status in
Canada years prior.  On his U.S. asylum
application, he changed his backstory,
including his birth date and clan affiliation.6
Then “[i]n 2001, authorities became aware of the
discrepancies surrounding Jamal’s immigration
history, and he was eventually convicted of lying to
immigration officials.  Jamal was sentenced to one
year of probation and referred for deportation.  The
standing deportation order has followed Jamal since
its issuance in 2011.” Id.
Unfortunately for American taxpayers, and the
safety of our neighborhoods, Jamal’s story of
defrauding the asylum system is hardly unique.
Indeed, as Louis Crocetti, the Former Associate
Director of Fraud Detection and National Security for
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (“USCIS”),
testified to Congress in 2014, one study showed that 12
percent of asylum applications studied were
6 Mia Cathell, “How the self-appointed spokesman of Minnesota’s
Somali community duped friendly media and convicted
fraudsters,” Washington Examiner (Oct. 5, 2026).

16
conclusively determined to be fraudulent, and fully 58
percent had “possible indicators of fraud.”7
According to the Department of Homeland
Security, more than 170,000 aliens were granted
asylum in the United States during a period
comparable to the Biden administration.8  In 2021,
“The leading countries of nationality for refugees
admitted ... were the Democratic Republic of the
Congo, Syria, and Afghanistan.”9  In 2022, the leading
countries were “the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
Syria, and Burma.”10  In 2023, the leading countries
were “Afghanistan, the People’s Republic of China
(China), and Venezuela.”11  And in 2024, the leading
countries were “Afghanistan, China, and Russia.”12
A 2015 report by the Government Accountability
Office (“GAO”) noted that the Departments of Justice
7 Louis Crocetti, “Testimony Before the House Judiciary
